title: Industry Pulse — AI / Agent Ecosystem

bullets.title: THE DAY'S LEAD — an active MCP supply-chain campaign that defeats review by construction. "Deadbugz" ships a benign MCP server, waits for exactly three tool calls, then rewrites the tool metadata it returns into instructions to hunt SSH keys, AWS credentials, shell history and Kubernetes config — and to hide the activity from the user
bullets.summary: Primary digest fetched; published 2026-09-07T06:00Z, in window by hours. Campaign documented by Pillar Security and described as currently active. Verbatim: the server "offers text formatting and summarization, then, after exactly three tool calls, rewrites the metadata it returns into instructions to hunt for SSH keys, AWS credentials, shell history, and Kubernetes config while concealing the activity from the user." Distribution was brute-force: one GitHub account filed 23 pull requests across unrelated AI and developer-tool projects in 74 minutes, the server calling itself productivity-suite. The framing that matters: "the metadata that turns into instructions hunting SSH keys and cloud credentials only appears once the server is trusted and in use," therefore "Deadbugz makes a one-time review structurally insufficient. A server that behaves for three calls and then changes its tool descriptions passes every check you run before approving it." IOCs published — endpoint, local artifact path, repository.
bullets.how: YES — the most directly actionable item in two weeks, because it is an attack against the exact configuration The Construct runs. This session alone loads ~20 MCP servers, mostly third-party, several OAuth-connected to live business systems (Slack, Gmail, Drive, Canva, Quartr, financial data, media generation). Every one was approved once and trusted since. The defence needs no vendor cooperation and is one comparison: cache tool definitions at approval and diff them on every reconnect, alerting on drift. The secondary recommendation — an authorization layer so a hijacked agent inherits a narrow surface — lands on the same nerve as the Aug 22 MCP roadmap: our credential model is one person approving in a browser, once, forever.

bullets.title: AND THE POPULATION NUMBER UNDERNEATH IT — a scaled active audit of internet-facing MCP servers finds 91.8% with no authentication at all, and 687 tool instances exposing shell execution with no access control. The three August MCP CVEs are all classic web flaws with no model involved
bullets.summary: Passive discovery across eleven sources feeding an active framework of 34 test modules over ten MCP-specific vulnerability classes. Of 640 confirmed production servers, 414 audited and 68 reportable vulnerabilities surfaced — SQL injection, SSRF against cloud metadata services, prompt template injection, path traversal via cursor manipulation. Posture is worse than the vuln count: 91.8% had no authentication whatsoever; 687 tool instances exposed shell execution with no access control. And 41.6% of discovered servers vanished within three days, so an MCP endpoint registry is a snapshot with a half-life, not a stable asset list. CVEs: CVE-2026-73498 path traversal in the Atlassian MCP (confluence_upload_attachment passes a client-supplied path straight to open(file_path,'rb'), arbitrary file read, CVSS 7.7, fixed v0.22.0); CVE-2026-67357 ArcadeDB MCP returns the HA cluster token in cleartext via a settings tool, enough to impersonate root, CVSS 7.7, fixed 26.7.3; CVE-2026-19956 SSRF in facebook-ads-mcp-server, CVSS 5.3. "Three August MCP CVEs, three classic web flaw classes, zero of them involving a model at all."
bullets.how: YES. Bullet 1 is the exotic threat; this is the boring one, and the boring one is likelier. Our exposure is not running an internet-facing MCP server — we do not — it is CONSUMING them, and a consumed server with no auth in front of it is a server anyone else can consume too. First pass is an inventory with two columns this report has never asked for: who authenticates the caller, and what the server can reach if the caller is not us.

bullets.title: /skill-doctor IS SHIPPED, IN HAND, AND WAS NEVER PENDING — it landed in 2.1.261 on September 4, and the changelog holds with NO September 7 release. Also in that build: an auto-mode default change that treats a diagram-renderer link as an upload
bullets.summary: Primary fetched and parsed by version heading rather than read as prose, per the standing rule after date failure #9. Top of page in order: 2.1.263 / Sep 6 (body still the single line "Bug fixes and reliability improvements"), 2.1.261 / Sep 4, 2.1.260 / Sep 3, 2.1.259 / Sep 2, 2.1.258 and 2.1.257 / Sep 1, 2.1.252 / Aug 31, 2.1.251 / Aug 28. No September 7 entry exists, and the gaps are wider than previously recorded: 2.1.262 absent, and 2.1.253 through 2.1.256 absent. The finding is in 2.1.261, verbatim: "Added /skill-doctor to show which loaded skills go unused and what they cost in context, so you can prune them." Nine days were spent treating a skill-context audit as blocked on a version upgrade; the purpose-built command has been in a shipped release since Friday. Same build: bashOutputMaxChars and taskOutputMaxChars raise inline command and background-task output up to 128K characters before spilling to a file, and --append-subagent-system-prompt-file reads a subagent system prompt from a file "for prompts too large to pass on the command line." Plus one security-shaped default: "Changed auto mode to treat a link that packs content into a public diagram renderer's URL as an upload to that site: no longer auto-approved unless you asked for it."
bullets.how: YES. Run /skill-doctor against the ~130-skill corpus this week — cheapest of the three measurements and the only one that names the skills. The 128K output settings matter for the render and deploy jobs that currently truncate. And the diagram-renderer change is bullet 1 in miniature: the vendor has decided content leaving the machine inside a URL is an upload regardless of what the UI calls it, and our own corpus builds diagrams that way.

bullets.title: HOW the tools are shaped changes behaviour as much as WHAT they do — 11,700 trajectories across six tool architectures with capability held constant: structured low-level interfaces improve consistency up to 4.7x, and CodeAct-style Python interfaces hit the same task performance with 41.6% fewer steps and 56.3% lower token usage
bullets.summary: Primary abstract fetched; submitted 11 Aug 2026, out of window, named for the reading queue not as news. 'The Devil Is in the Interface' (Xu, Saghir, Wu, Cote, Wang, Lakkaraju, Pei, Zhang) isolates a variable this fleet has never controlled for: not which capabilities an agent has, but how they are organised and exposed. Holding underlying information and actions similar across six architectures and three actors: versus a bash-only baseline, more structured low-level interfaces improve consistency across repeated attempts by up to 4.7x; natural-language search broadens repository exploration and increases access to relevant files by more than 11%; Python CodeAct-style interfaces achieve similar task performance with 41.6% fewer steps and 56.3% lower token usage. The negative result stings: "lightweight text-based cognitive-scaffolding tools, such as tools that let the agent record intermediate reasoning, have limited effect on actor behavior."
bullets.how: MAYBE tending to YES, and it slots behind bullet 3 rather than competing. /skill-doctor answers WHICH skills are dead weight; yesterday's canary paper (2608.04719) answers whether the live ones are SELECTED correctly; this answers whether they are SHAPED correctly, and is the only one that puts a token number on the prize. Note what it quietly deprecates: a meaningful share of our ~130 skills are prose scaffolds telling an agent to record reasoning or follow a checklist — the controlled result says that class changes behaviour least.

bullets.title: THIRD FIRE (13:55 ET) — the report has been collecting the pieces of two patterns without naming either: every frontier lab shipped or announced a CYBER-CAPABLE model in one week and rationed access to all of them, and Deadbugz is not a novel attack but an instance of a class the NSA and DoD named in a joint advisory on June 2
bullets.summary: Two independent surfaces converge on a pattern this report published only in fragments. PATTERN ONE — the cyber convergence: in a single week OpenAI declared Astra "the first to meet its internal Critical cybersecurity threshold," Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber to a trusted-defender program (Fairwind), and Anthropic released Mythos 5.1 through restricted access. Verbatim framing: "The labs are shipping offensive-grade capability and rationing it." This report carried Gemini Cyber on the second fire as an OMISSION and Mythos 5.1 for a week as a routine release; it never noticed they were the same move by three vendors. PATTERN TWO — Deadbugz has a name and a date that precede it: on 2026-06-02 the NSA and US Department of Defense issued a joint advisory identifying TOOL POISONING, RUG PULL ATTACKS and CROSS-SERVER TRUST EXPLOITATION as priority risk categories for organizations deploying agentic AI. A rug pull is defined as exactly what Deadbugz does: "a previously clean server pushes an update that adds poisoned content, and the host agent reloads tool descriptions without re-prompting." Documented prior incidents: Postmark's official MCP server silently BCC'd every sent email to the maintainer's address; Smithery's path traversal exposed deployment credentials for over 3,000 hosted MCP apps. CALENDAR — Microsoft runs "MCP Live!" on 2026-09-09, 16:00-20:00 UTC, a half-day livestream whose stated scope is enterprise readiness: authentication, governance, security. NULLS re-confirmed on a third pass and unchanged: no Sep 7 Claude Code release (2.1.263 / Sep 6 remains newest), no Sep 7 Anthropic first-party item, no frontier release since GPT-6 Astra (Sep 3), no in-window agent funding round, no new MCP protocol-blog post since the Aug 22 roadmap. SIGNAGE: the July 31 Signage Details dataset is unread at source for a THIRD consecutive fire and is the oldest open action here.
bullets.how: YES on both patterns, and the second one is a correction to this morning's own lead. The cyber convergence is a PRAGMA positioning asset and a procurement warning at once: the capability tier that matters for defending an agent fleet is now gated behind vendor trust programs, so the question for The Construct is not whether to buy it but whether we can qualify for it — worth an application to Google's Fairwind Program on the strength of the MCP fleet we actually operate. The Deadbugz reframing is more uncomfortable: this report led with it at 06:00 as though it were new, when the attack class was named by the NSA three months ago and has documented victims. That does not weaken the action — cache tool definitions at approval, diff on every reconnect, alert on drift — it strengthens it, because the defence is now a documented control against a government-named risk category rather than a reaction to one blog post. Put MCP Live! on the calendar for Wednesday; enterprise MCP auth and governance is the exact gap bullets 1 and 2 opened.

praxis_lesson: Yesterday's rule was that a null must name the surface it was read from. One day of applying it produces a sharper version, because naming the surface was not sufficient: the frontier null names llmgateway.io/timeline honestly, and the page itself says "Updated September 3, 2026." Five consecutive days of "no frontier release" were five days of reading a page that stopped being written on the third. So a null must name its surface AND that surface's own last-updated date, and where the surface is staler than the window, the finding is not "null" but "unverified" — a different word, because it licenses a different action. Null means nothing happened and you may stop looking. Unverified means the channel failed and you must look elsewhere. This report has been publishing the first while earning only the second, and the distinction costs one line per bullet. Second, and larger: Deadbugz changes what approval IS. A server that behaves for three tool calls and then rewrites its own tool descriptions into credential-hunting instructions means a security review is not a gate an artifact passes, it is a timestamped observation of a thing that is free to change afterwards — every check run before trusting a server tests a version of that server chosen by the server. The corpus has the same shape in miniature: skills are self-authored, edited between sessions, never re-read after first approval, and the fleet's MCP servers were each approved once by a person in a browser and trusted ever since. The defence is embarrassingly cheap — hash the tool definitions and skill descriptions at approval, diff on every reconnect, alert on drift — and its cheapness is the argument. Third, the week's three measurements finally stack in the right order and none is blocked: /skill-doctor (shipped Sep 4, names the dead weight), canary probes (2608.04719, tests whether live skills are selected correctly), tool architecture (2608.11386, tests whether they are shaped correctly, and quantifies the prize at 41.6% fewer steps and 56.3% fewer tokens). Nine days were lost waiting for the first to arrive. It had arrived. The pattern to break is not slow tooling — it is a report that keeps checking whether a capability exists instead of running it.  AMENDED AT THE SECOND FIRE (10:00 ET): the morning rule was right and incomplete. "Unverified" was the correct verdict on a stale channel, but it is only half a procedure — flagging a channel as dead is worthless unless the same pass goes to a SECOND SURFACE, and the flag is not cleared by waiting, it is cleared by reading somewhere else. Twenty minutes of doing that resolved a flag this report was about to carry for a sixth day, and the resolution was the undramatic one: the null was true all along. That is the failure mode worth naming, because it is the INVERSE of the one we keep guarding against. Nine logged date failures are all cases where a stale source made old news look new. This was a stale source producing a CORRECT answer — the most dangerous kind, because it is never caught by checking whether the answer is wrong; it is caught only by checking whether the channel is alive, independently of whether you like its answer. Second, the omissions are the real yield and they share one cause: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and Anthropic's EFS were both published September 2, both squarely on this report's beat, and neither was missed because it was hard to find — each was missed because A SINGLE SURFACE WAS TREATED AS A CENSUS. A null sweep read off one page per category is not a sweep, it is one page's opinion, and it fails silently in both directions: it invents absences and it hides presences. The count that matters is not how many days a negative has held but HOW MANY INDEPENDENT SURFACES HAVE BEEN ASKED, and until today that answer was one. Third, the recovered items change the week's actions: Google shipped an access-gated defender-only security model in the same week an active MCP supply-chain campaign was documented, and Anthropic shipped an architecture where the customer holds the data and the vendor holds only the detector. Action list unchanged in order but now owner-facing: run /skill-doctor, hash-and-diff the MCP tool definitions, READ THE JULY 31 SIGNAGE DETAILS ANNOUNCEMENT AT SOURCE (day two, oldest open item), and file EFS under PRAGMA positioning rather than news.  AMENDED AT THE THIRD FIRE (13:55 ET): the second fire's rule was that a single surface treated as a census is not a sweep. Applying it a third time produces the rule that supersedes both, and it is not about surfaces at all — it is about TIME. This report led at 06:00 with Deadbugz as "the most directly actionable item in two weeks," and it is; but it is an instance of RUG PULL, an attack class the NSA and DoD named in a joint advisory on 2026-06-02, with documented victims (Postmark, Smithery) predating today by months. Nothing in the morning report was false. What was wrong was the FRAME: a daily scan is structurally biased toward treating the newest ARTICLE about a thing as the arrival of the thing, because its whole job is to find what is new in 24 hours, and a 24-hour window cannot see a three-month-old advisory that would have told us to build the defence in June. So the rule is: BEFORE CALLING AN ITEM A LEAD, ASK WHAT CLASS IT BELONGS TO AND WHEN THAT CLASS WAS FIRST NAMED. If the class is older than the window, the news is not the attack — the news is that we did not act when the class was named, and the report should say so in those words. Second, the same time-blindness hid a pattern in plain sight. Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber was logged as an omission, Mythos 5.1 as a routine release, OpenAI Astra as a frontier entry — three separate bullets across three fires, when they are one event: every major lab shipped offensive-grade cyber capability in a single week and gated all of it behind trust programs. A report structured as a list of items will reliably miss a pattern made of items, because nothing in the format asks "what do these three have in common." The fix is one question per sweep, asked of the whole day rather than of any bullet. Third, the action list is unchanged in content and now has a deadline attached: run /skill-doctor, hash-and-diff the MCP tool definitions (now justified as a control against a government-named risk category, not a blog post), attend or record Microsoft's MCP Live! on Wednesday September 9 for enterprise MCP auth and governance, investigate qualifying for Google's Fairwind defender program, and READ THE JULY 31 SIGNAGE DETAILS ANNOUNCEMENT AT SOURCE — unread across three consecutive fires and now indefensible.
